extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, PTO disciplinary counsel, and administrative adjudicators
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules applied in a USPTO disciplinary proceeding resulting in default, covering methods of service, due-process notice, misconduct definitions under 37 C.F.R. Part 10, and factors for assessing discipline and sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of serving a complaint (37 C.F.R. § 11.35(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A complaint may be served on a respondent by: (1) delivering a copy personally to the respondent; or (2) mailing a copy by 'Express Mail,' first-class mail, or any delivery service that provides ability to confirm delivery or attempted delivery to a respondent who is a registered practitioner at the address provided to OED pursuant to § 11.11.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If service by the methods in paragraph (a) cannot be accomplished, Rule 11.35(b) provides alternate procedures (publication). The page describes multiple compliant attempts to serve by mail (including certified mail) to addresses on file and to institutional/inmate addresses; service by these enumerated postal/delivery methods is authorized and is the baseline for evaluating sufficiency of service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication service when other methods fail (37 C.F.R. § 11.35(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: If a copy of the complaint cannot be delivered through the procedures in paragraph (a), the OED Director shall serve the respondent by causing an appropriate notice to be published in the Official Gazette for two consecutive weeks, in which case the time for filing an answer shall be thirty days from the second publication of the notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to timely file an answer after publication constitutes an admission of the allegations and may lead to entry of an initial decision on default. The requirement and the 30-day answer period from second publication are treated as binding procedural triggers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to notify OED of address changes (37 C.F.R. § 11.11(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Registered attorneys must notify the OED Director of the address of their office and any changes to that address within thirty days of the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although § 11.11 technically requires notice of office-address changes, the decision emphasizes that practitioners who want to receive communications from PTO should provide current addresses; failure to do so can weigh against them when assessing whether service was reasonably calculated to notify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completion of service by mail for papers other than a complaint (37 C.F.R. § 11.42(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Service by mail is completed when the paper mailed in the United States is placed into the custody of the U.S. Postal Service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted delivery methods include personal delivery, first-class mail, Express Mail, other delivery service, or another mutually agreeable method (see § 11.42(b)(1)-(3)). The decision treats mailing (e.g., certified mail) that is placed in USPS custody as completed service even if later returned 'unclaimed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Time for answer and default judgment (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(a),(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: An answer to a complaint shall be filed within the time set in the complaint but in no event less than thirty days from the date the complaint is filed. Failure to timely file an answer will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in entry of default judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule does not require a separate motion for default nor fix a minimum period to respond to a motion for default. The decision treats the respondent's failure to answer within the applicable period as grounds for entering default and deeming allegations admitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process standard for notice (Mullane/Dusenbery standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Due process requires 'notice reasonably calculated, under all the circumstances, to apprise interested parties of the pendency of the action and afford them an opportunity to present their objections' (Mullane). Prior cases (e.g., Dusenbery) confirm that the Constitution does not require proof of actual receipt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Service on a prison official or mailing to a forwarding address provided by USPS can satisfy due process if the attempts were reasonably calculated under the circumstances. The tribunal evaluates the quality and reasonableness of attempts at service rather than actual receipt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness of attempts to effectuate service (judging quality of attempts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tribunal should assess whether the means employed were such as one desirous of actually informing the respondent might reasonably adopt to accomplish it (citing Mullane).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sending to inmate address provided by corrections official, delivering to prison counselor, using USPS forwarding address and certified mail, and leaving notice are all relevant. The decision notes USPS Domestic Mail Manual distinctions (e.g., 'unclaimed' vs 'Moved, Left No Address') when judging whether returned mail undermines sufficiency of service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default consequences: admission of allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to timely file an answer constitutes an admission of the allegations in the complaint and the respondent is deemed to have admitted all of the allegations in the complaint pursuant to Rules 11.35(b) and 11.36(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entry of default permits the hearing officer to render findings and conclusions based on the allegations alone and proceed to disposition (including sanctions) without a contested evidentiary record from the respondent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misconduct definitions and prohibitions (37 C.F.R. § 10.23)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 10.23 provides: (a) A practitioner shall not engage in disreputable or gross misconduct. (b) A practitioner shall not: (3) engage in illegal conduct involving moral turpitude; (4) engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation; (6) engage in any other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office. (c) Conduct constituting violation includes, but is not limited to, (1) conviction of a criminal offense involving moral turpitude, dishonesty, or breach of trust; (5) suspension or disbarment on ethical grounds by any duly constituted authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision applies these subsections to conduct such as a felony conviction for theft from a client trust account and to subsequent suspension/disbarment by the State Bar. It also explains that subsection (b)(6) (other conduct) is not an appropriate separate finding when the conduct already falls within other enumerated grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of state conviction/suspension as grounds (10.23(c)(1), (c)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Conviction of a criminal offense involving moral turpitude, dishonesty, or breach of trust and suspension/disbarment by a state on ethical grounds constitute violations of Rule 10.23(a) and (b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: conviction for grand theft from client trust account constitutes moral turpitude/dishonesty/breach of trust; state suspension/disbarment based on such a conviction qualifies as discipline under § 10.23(c)(5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider in imposing penalty (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining any penalty, consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused by the misconduct; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision analyzes these factors: theft from a client violates duties of trust and loyalty and duty to the public; the misconduct was knowingly and willfully committed; actual financial harm may be minimal if restitution made but potential injury was significant; mitigating factors may be limited. Relevant precedent and ABA Standards (e.g., 4.11, 4.12) are used to inform sanction selection (disbarment for knowing conversion, suspension for lesser offenses). Because default prevented full record development, the tribunal elected indeterminate suspension until reinstatement procedures are engaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ABA Standards and case precedent in sanctioning
rubrics_metrics.description: The tribunal may rely on American Bar Association Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions and case law to guide appropriate sanctions—e.g., ABA Standard 4.11 (disbarment appropriate when lawyer knowingly converts client property causing injury or potential injury) and 4.12 (suspension appropriate when lawyer knows or should know she is dealing improperly with client property and causes injury or potential injury).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision cites state cases (In re Ennenga; In re Blumenstyk; In re Wilson) holding knowing misappropriation ordinarily warrants disbarment, but notes that absence of a full record (due to default) may justify a less final sanction such as indeterminate suspension pending further showing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referral upon final order imposing interim suspension (37 C.F.R. § 11.25(b)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon entering a final order imposing interim suspension, the USPTO Director shall refer the complaint to a hearing officer to conduct a formal disciplinary proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issuance of the Final Order triggers the timeline for filing an answer with the hearing officer (30 days) and activates referral to the adjudicator who will conduct the formal proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-discipline obligations and reinstatement references (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58, 11.60)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplined practitioners are subject to the responsibilities in § 11.58; petitions for reinstatement are governed by § 11.60.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision directs respondent's attention to these provisions (rules govern obligations of disciplined practitioners and procedures to seek reinstatement) though it does not elaborate their content on the face of the decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal procedure and timing (37 C.F.R. § 11.55)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any appeal from the Initial Decision must be filed with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office within 30 days after the decision, must include exceptions to the Administrative Law Judge's Decision and supporting reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to file an appeal in accordance with § 11.55 is deemed acceptance of the Initial Decision and waiver of rights to further administrative and judicial review.
